passages.text: For decades, wealthy democracies had treated foreign aid as a modest but durable fixture of their budgets, a commitment that weathered the vagaries of changing governments with only minor adjustments. That consensus fractured with startling speed in 2025. On its first day in office, the new administration in Washington ordered a ninety-day pause on most foreign assistance. The United States Agency for International Development, which had managed the bulk of America's humanitarian and development programs, was soon being dismantled. A month later, the British government announced that it would shrink aid from 0.5 to 0.3 percent of national income by 2027 and redirect the savings to defense, and several other European donors pared their own budgets. Proponents of the retrenchment argue that governments must prioritize their own citizens. In their view, aid has too often entrenched dependence rather than fostering self-sufficiency. Detractors counter that the sums involved are a minuscule share of national spending, while their absence is acutely felt. Clinics distributing HIV medication, vaccination drives, and famine early-warning systems rely on predictable funding, and such funding cannot be conjured overnight. Some economists add a more pragmatic objection. Aid, they note, has long been an inexpensive instrument of influence, and when established donors retreat, rival powers are seldom loath to fill the vacuum.

Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today, only a tiny fraction is well represented in the vast troves of text used to train large language models. English alone accounts for a large share of the material on the public internet. Chatbots that converse eloquently in English or Mandarin often falter in Yoruba, Quechua, or Lao. They produce stilted phrasing or outright errors. Researchers call such languages low-resource. The label describes not their expressive richness but the paucity of digitized text. The disparity matters because AI systems are rapidly being woven into public services, from medical triage to legal advice. Speakers of underserved languages may be nudged toward a dominant tongue simply to be understood by the machine, and such pressure could precipitate the decline of languages already under strain. Yet the same technology offers a glimmer of hope. Community groups have begun chronicling elders, transcribing oral narratives, and compiling modest datasets on their own terms, sometimes insisting on licenses that keep control in local hands. Whether AI ultimately ____ linguistic diversity may therefore depend less on the algorithms themselves than on who gathers the data and who decides how it is used.

Ask adults how much their tastes, values, and personalities have changed over the past decade, and most will readily concede that they are quite different people from who they once were. Ask the same adults how much they expect to change over the next decade, however, and their predictions shrink precipitously. In a study published in 2013, psychologists surveyed more than nineteen thousand participants. They found this asymmetry at every age they examined, from young adults to people in their late sixties. The researchers dubbed it the end of history illusion: the persistent belief that the person one is today is, at last, the finished version. One plausible explanation concerns effort. Recalling past change is easy, since memories supply ready evidence. Imagining future change is laborious, and the absence of a vivid image is mistaken for the absence of change itself. The illusion carries practical costs. Participants said they would pay considerably more to see their current favorite band perform a decade from now than to see a once-beloved band perform today. Recognizing the illusion need not paralyze decision-making, but it does counsel humility. When committing to choices that are difficult to reverse, we would do well to remember that the self who must live with them has not yet arrived.

Shop signs promising Ye Olde Tea Shoppe are meant to evoke a quaint medieval past, but their very first word rests on a misunderstanding. Old and Middle English possessed a letter called thorn, which represented the sound now spelled th. When printing reached England in the 1470s, the typefaces available had been cast on the Continent, where no language required thorn, so printers were forced to (A) ____. Some substituted the pair th, but others used y, whose handwritten form had come to resemble thorn closely. Thus ye, in phrases such as ye olde, was simply a printed abbreviation of the. It was pronounced exactly as the is today. Readers of later centuries were unfamiliar with the convention and took the y at face value. In modern times the pronunciation yee has become a playful marker of antiquity. Thorn was not the only casualty of the transition from manuscript to print. Its companion eth stood for the same sounds and had fallen into desuetude long before. The letter yogh, used for various guttural sounds, gave way to combinations such as gh, leaving English with silent letters in words like night and though. The episode illustrates how technology can quietly reshape a writing system. Decisions made by a handful of printers, constrained by the type they happened to own, hardened into conventions that later generations treated as (B) ____, mistaking accidents of equipment for features of the language itself.

The goal of ten thousand steps a day is so widely repeated that many people assume it emerged from medical research. In fact, its origins lie largely in marketing. Around the time of the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, a Japanese company deftly marketed a pedometer whose name translated roughly as ten-thousand-step meter, a round figure that was memorable and, conveniently, ambitious. The number later proliferated through fitness trackers and public health campaigns around the world, acquiring an aura of scientific precision it had never earned. When researchers finally scrutinized it, the results were instructive. A 2019 study of older women found that those who walked about 4,400 steps a day had markedly lower mortality than the least active women. The benefits leveled off at around 7,500 steps. A later analysis pooled data from several countries and reported broadly similar plateaus, generally between six and eight thousand steps for adults over sixty and somewhat higher for younger adults. None of this means that walking more is deleterious, and additional steps may still improve fitness. But the findings suggest that an arbitrary target may dishearten sedentary people who regard it as unattainable. Far more modest increases would bring substantial gains. The most important steps, it appears, are simply the first few thousand.

The distinctive scent that rises from dry ground after the first rain of a season received its name only in 1964. That year two Australian chemists called it petrichor. The word comes from the Greek words for stone and for the fluid said to flow in the veins of the gods. Much of the aroma emanates from geosmin, a compound produced by soil bacteria, and the human nose is extraordinarily sensitive to it, detecting it at a few parts per trillion. How the scent becomes airborne remained inscrutable until 2015. Engineers using high-speed cameras then showed that raindrops striking porous soil trap tiny pockets of air, which rise through the drop and burst into a fine aerosol. Light rain on sandy or clay soil releases the most aerosol. This explains why a gentle shower can smell more pungent than a downpour. Why our noses should be so finely attuned to geosmin is less certain. One hypothesis holds that sensitivity to the smell of wet earth helped our ancestors locate water in arid landscapes. Recent research on springtails, minuscule soil animals that are drawn to geosmin and in turn disperse the bacteria's spores, suggests that the compound may be ____ rather than a mere by-product.

Rembrandt's The Night Watch, completed in 1642, is among the most celebrated paintings in the Netherlands. Yet the canvas visitors admire today is not the one Rembrandt delivered. In 1715 Ⓐ<u>the enormous group portrait</u> was moved to the town hall of Amsterdam. It proved too large for the wall assigned to it, so strips were trimmed from all four sides, the widest from the left. Two figures at the edge vanished entirely. The composition had originally placed the striding captain slightly off-center to convey forward movement, but after the cut it became noticeably more static. The excised pieces have never been found. Our knowledge of what is missing comes largely from a much smaller copy painted before the cut by Gerrit Lundens, a contemporary. Even the familiar title is a later accretion, for the scene was not set at night at all. Over time Ⓑ<u>the painting</u> darkened under layers of varnish and grime, inspiring a nickname that stuck. The Rijksmuseum, which has displayed Ⓒ<u>the work</u> since the late nineteenth century, unveiled an unusual reconstruction in 2021. Researchers trained a computer program on Rembrandt's brushwork and palette and used Ⓓ<u>the copy</u> as a guide to generate the missing strips, which were printed and mounted temporarily around the original. The project did not pretend to restore Rembrandt's own hand. Its aim was more modest: to let viewers glimpse, for a few months, the sense of movement that a mundane decision about wall space had quietly erased three centuries earlier.

Can smiling make you happier? The idea that facial expressions not only reflect emotions but also shape them has a long pedigree. Both Charles Darwin and William James entertained versions of it. In 1988 a team of German psychologists concocted an ingenious test. To keep participants from guessing the purpose of the study, they asked them to hold a pen either between their teeth or between their lips. The first position forces the face into something resembling a smile, and the second prevents one. Participants in the first condition rated cartoons as funnier, and the experiment became a staple of introductory textbooks. In 2016, however, seventeen laboratories repeated the procedure with nearly two thousand participants and found no effect at all. The failure was widely cited as an emblem of psychology's replication crisis. Yet the story did not end there. The original author pointed out that participants in the new studies had been filmed, and a later experiment suggested that the effect appeared only when no camera was present, perhaps because being observed makes people self-conscious. In 2022 an international collaboration involving thousands of participants in many countries reported that deliberately posing a smile produced a small but detectable increase in happiness. The emerging picture is more ____ than either the original enthusiasm or the subsequent dismissal: our faces may nudge our feelings, but only slightly, and only under certain conditions.

Students preparing for examinations tend to favor rereading their notes and highlighting textbooks, strategies that feel productive because the material grows increasingly familiar. Familiarity, however, is a treacherous guide to learning. A large body of research indicates that retrieving information from memory, rather than reviewing it, consolidates it most durably. In one well-known experiment, students read a prose passage and then tried to recall it in writing. A week later they remembered considerably more than students who had spent the same time rereading, even though the rereaders had predicted they would perform better. Psychologists call this the testing effect. It belongs to a broader family of what one researcher termed desirable difficulties. These are conditions that make learning feel slower and more arduous in the moment but yield sturdier retention. Spacing study sessions apart rather than cramming is another example. So is interleaving different kinds of problems rather than practicing one kind in a block. The paradox is that learners gauge their progress by fluency, the ease with which material comes to mind while it lies in front of them, and fluency is precisely what these effective techniques sacrifice. Teachers who adopt frequent low-stakes quizzes must therefore try to persuade students that the discomfort of struggling to remember is not a symptom of failure but the very mechanism of learning.

Few words seem as breezy and informal as ciao, the greeting that Italians use both on meeting and on parting. It has spread into dozens of other languages. Its origins, however, are surprisingly servile. The word comes from the Venetian dialect, in which s-ciavo meant slave, derived from the medieval Latin sclavus. For centuries, Venetians greeted one another with a phrase roughly meaning I am your slave, a courteous formula of deference comparable to the English your humble servant, which once closed formal letters. Through ceaseless repetition, the expression was worn down to a single syllable. Its original meaning faded from awareness, much as few English speakers today hear God be with you inside goodbye. By the twentieth century, ciao had spread from northern Italy across the country and shed any trace of formality. It became the casual greeting reserved for friends and family, while strangers were addressed more formally. A similar transformation occurred in parts of central Europe, where servus, the Latin word for slave, survives as a friendly hello. These histories illustrate a recurring pattern in language: expressions of exaggerated ____ tend, through overuse, to become ordinary pleasantries, their literal content quietly drained away.

Ask a room of teachers whether students learn better when lessons match their preferred learning style, whether visual, auditory, or kinesthetic, and most hands will go up. Surveys in several countries have found that a large majority of educators endorse the idea. An industry of questionnaires, workshops, and classroom materials has burgeoned around it. The appeal is easy to understand. People do have preferences, and tailoring instruction to each child sounds both scientific and humane. The claim at the heart of the theory, however, <u>does not survive contact with the evidence</u>. To demonstrate it, a study would need to sort learners by style, teach each group in several ways, and show that each learns best when instruction matches its style. In 2008 a team of cognitive psychologists reviewed the research. Very few studies had used such a design, and those that had largely failed to find the predicted pattern. Later experiments reached similar conclusions. Students who describe themselves as visual learners do not remember more from pictures than from words, compared with students who claim other styles. What does matter is the fit between the method and the material. A map conveys geography better than a spoken description for nearly everyone, just as pronunciation is best learned by listening. Critics of the myth argue that it is subtly deleterious: it can encourage students to shun challenging modes of learning and divert teachers' limited time toward matching lessons to labels.

For a time, the name of a piece of software became a verb. In the late 2000s people spoke of skyping relatives abroad, and the program's free calls over the internet seemed little short of miraculous to families accustomed to paying extortionate rates for international telephone calls. Launched in 2003 by Scandinavian entrepreneurs working with Estonian engineers, Skype routed calls directly between users' computers, a design that kept its costs remarkably low. Its success attracted (A) ____ buyers: the auction company eBay acquired it in 2005. Microsoft bought it in 2011 for roughly eight and a half billion dollars, at the time the largest acquisition in its history. Yet in May 2025 Microsoft shut Skype down and directed its remaining users to its workplace application, Teams. The decline had been gradual and then sudden. Smartphones favored messaging apps that were built for mobile devices from the start, while Skype, designed for desktop computers, floundered. When the pandemic sent billions of people online in 2020, it was a younger rival, Zoom, that became the default for remote meetings and classes. Part of the reason was that joining a call required nothing more than clicking a link. Analysts glean several lessons from the episode. Being first confers no permanent advantage; a product's architecture can become a liability when the technology around it shifts. And ownership by a large company does not guarantee survival, particularly when the parent is focused elsewhere. Skype's fate is a reminder of how (B) ____ dominance in consumer technology can be.

Every time a European shopper buys from an American website or a hospital consults software hosted abroad, personal data crosses a border. Governments are increasingly zealous about controlling where it goes. The European Union's data protection regulation, in force since 2018, countenances transfers of personal information to other countries only if it will receive protection commensurate with that guaranteed at home. Twice, Europe's highest court has struck down arrangements for the free flow of such data to the United States. In the court's view, American surveillance law afforded Europeans scant recourse. A new framework replaced those arrangements in 2023, and in the same year Meta was fined 1.2 billion euros for transfers made under the earlier rules. Other governments have espoused their own versions of data sovereignty. Some mandate the domestic storage of certain categories of information, while others subject exports of data to stringent security reviews. Advocates contend that such rules are the only way to keep privacy rights from evaporating at the border. Critics decry the prospect of a splintering internet. Firms would have to duplicate infrastructure in each jurisdiction, and small companies would be priced out of international markets. The free flow of information behind the internet's growth would be supplanted by a patchwork of incompatible regimes.

Many workers are familiar with the slump of the early afternoon, when concentration wavers and eyelids grow heavy. The dip is often imputed to lunch. In fact it is largely built into the body's daily rhythm and occurs even when the midday meal is skipped. A brief nap is among the most efficacious remedies. In a well-known study for NASA in the 1990s, long-haul pilots were allowed a planned rest of forty minutes in the cockpit while a colleague flew the aircraft. They slept about twenty-five minutes and afterward displayed markedly better alertness and performance than pilots with no rest. The benefits depend heavily on timing and length, however. Sleep researchers generally recommend naps of ten to twenty minutes in the early afternoon. Longer naps allow the sleeper to descend into deep sleep, and waking from that stage produces sleep inertia, a groggy disorientation that can linger for half an hour and temporarily impair judgment. Late naps can also hamper sleep at night. Some aficionados recommend drinking coffee immediately before a short nap, since the caffeine takes effect just as the sleeper wakes. Employers once derided napping at work as a symptom of indolence. Now a growing number provide quiet rooms for the purpose, cognizant that a few minutes of rest can pay for themselves in safer and more productive work.

The word person has a theatrical lineage. In the theater of ancient Rome, actors wore masks to identify the characters they played, and the Latin term for such a mask was persona. A popular explanation, repeated since antiquity, derives the word from per sonare, to sound through, because the actor's voice resonated through the opening of the mask. Most modern linguists regard this etymology as spurious, since the vowel lengths do not match. Many surmise a borrowing from Etruscan, the language of Rome's northern neighbors, in which a similar word is associated with a masked figure. Whatever its origin, persona soon transcended the stage. Roman jurists used it for an individual who bears rights and duties. Early Christian theologians employed it in intricate debates about the nature of God. In the twentieth century the psychologist Carl Jung revived the word to describe the social face an individual presents to the world. Such a mask is expedient but perilous when mistaken for the whole self. The history is ____: the vocabulary we use for our innermost identity began as a term for something worn on the outside, a device for playing a role before an audience.

When economists tally the money that flows into developing countries, one source now (A) ____ the rest. Remittances, the funds that migrant workers send to relatives at home, amount to several hundred billion dollars a year, according to World Bank estimates. This exceeds foreign direct investment and official aid combined. In some smaller economies, they equal a quarter or more of national output. Unlike aid, which is channeled through governments and agencies, remittances go directly to households, where they pay for food, school fees, medical bills, and housing. They also tend to be remarkably resilient. When disaster strikes a home country, migrants often send more rather than less, cushioning the blow precisely when other forms of finance dry up. Yet the money comes at a cost, in more than one sense. Sending a small sum across borders still costs about six percent on average, double the target the United Nations has set for 2030. Fees are often highest on routes serving the most impoverished countries. Critics also fret that heavy reliance on remittances can relieve governments of pressure to create jobs at home, while the departure of young workers depletes villages of talent and leaves children to be raised by grandparents. Digital payment services have begun to whittle fees down. Some governments also offer incentives for migrants to invest their savings in local businesses. Whether remittances can do more than (B) ____ hardship, however, may depend on whether home countries build economies that give their citizens a reason to stay.

The white streaks that trail behind aircraft at cruising altitude are not smoke but ice. Contrails form when hot, humid exhaust meets the frigid air of the upper atmosphere, and in dry air they vanish within seconds. In air already saturated with moisture, however, they can persist for hours, diffusing into thin sheets of cirrus cloud. These artificial clouds exert an outsized effect on the climate. By day they reflect some sunlight back to space, but they also trap heat radiating from the earth. On balance they warm the planet, especially at night, when there is no sunlight to reflect. By some estimates, the warming from contrail clouds rivals or even exceeds that of the carbon dioxide emitted by aviation itself. Strikingly, a small fraction of flights produces most of this effect, because only certain layers of the atmosphere are humid enough to sustain long-lived contrails. That raises an intriguing possibility: airlines might obviate costly engine redesigns simply by adjusting altitudes to bypass such layers. In a 2023 trial, an airline and a technology company used forecasts to reroute several dozen flights and reported that contrails were cut by roughly half. Skeptics note that detours squander extra fuel and that forecasting humid layers remains imprecise. Still, the potential gains appear substantial relative to the cost.

Look up through the canopy of certain forests and you may see something anomalous. The crowns of neighboring trees stop just short of touching, leaving narrow channels of sky between them, like fissures in dried mud or the lines of a jigsaw puzzle. The phenomenon, known as crown shyness, has been noted by foresters since at least the 1920s. It is especially striking among camphor trees in Malaysia, though it occurs in many other species as well. Why trees should keep their distance remains a matter of conjecture. One explanation emphasizes wind. As tall, spindly trees sway, their outer branches strike those of their neighbors, snapping twigs and impairing growing buds, so that over time the gaps are effectively pruned into place. Studies of pines in windy locations found wider gaps between crowns that collided more often. Another explanation focuses on light. Plants can detect the altered light reflected by nearby leaves, and a branch that senses a neighbor may simply cease growing toward it, avoiding shade. A third suggestion is that the gaps forestall the spread of leaf-eating insects and disease from one tree to the next. These explanations are not mutually exclusive, and the pattern may well have ____ causes that vary from one forest to another.

Diego Velazquez's Las Meninas, painted in 1656 and hanging today in the Prado Museum in Madrid, has been called the most scrutinized painting in Western art. At first glance it seems a candid scene from the Spanish court. At the center stands Ⓐ<u>the five-year-old princess</u> Margarita Teresa, attended by two maids of honor, the meninas of the title, along with two dwarfs, a dog, and other members of the household. To the left, Ⓑ<u>the painter</u> himself stands before an enormous canvas with brush in hand and gazes out toward the viewer. But what he is painting is hidden from us, since we see only the back of the canvas. A small mirror on the rear wall offers a clue. It reflects the blurry figures of King Philip IV and Queen Mariana, who seem to be standing exactly where we stand. The viewer is thus drawn into an unsettling loop as both spectator and subject. Is Ⓒ<u>the artist</u> depicting the royal couple, the princess, or the very picture before us? Further intrigue surrounds the red cross on his chest, the emblem of a knightly order that Ⓓ<u>he</u> joined only in 1659, three years after the canvas was completed. The cross must have been added later. Centuries on, the work continues to provoke. Pablo Picasso painted a profusion of variations on it in 1957, and the philosopher Michel Foucault opened a celebrated book with an essay on its play of gazes, treating the painting as a meditation on representation itself.

During the pandemic, millions of office employees discovered that much of their work could be done from a kitchen table. Many employers, at first reluctantly, discovered the same. Since then the pendulum has been swinging back. In September 2024 Amazon told its corporate staff to be in the office five days a week from the start of 2025, and several large banks and technology firms issued similar edicts. Executives defending such mandates invoke intangible benefits: serendipitous conversations that engender ideas, the mentoring of junior colleagues who learn by watching, and a shared culture that is difficult to sustain over video calls. The evidence, however, is more ____ than either side tends to concede. A randomized experiment at a large Chinese travel company was published in 2024. Letting employees work from home two days a week cut resignations by about a third without harming performance or promotion prospects. Other studies suggest that fully remote arrangements can hamper the training of newcomers and erode collaboration across teams. Much depends on the nature of the work, the stage of an employee's career, and how deliberately an organization structures time together. Some observers also suspect that rigid mandates serve a tacit purpose. They may precipitate voluntary departures at a time when firms wish to trim payrolls without announcing layoffs. Whatever the motive, the debate has shifted from whether offices matter to a subtler question: what offices are for, and how often people must gather in them to obtain the benefits that justify the commute.

Most of us believe we understand how a zipper works, or a flush toilet, or a bicycle. In a series of experiments published in 2002, psychologists asked people to rate their understanding of such everyday devices, then to write a detailed, step-by-step explanation of how each one functions. After attempting the explanation, participants revised their ratings sharply downward. The researchers called this gap the illusion of explanatory depth. We conflate familiarity with an object, and the knowledge that its workings are known to someone, with an understanding we personally possess. The illusion is not confined to gadgets. Later studies asked people with strong opinions on political issues, such as a cap-and-trade system for carbon emissions, to explain precisely how the policy would operate. Struggling to delineate the mechanism, many became less certain and adopted more moderate positions. Notably, merely listing reasons for their views did not have the same effect. The distinction is instructive. Justifying a belief draws on arguments one has already rehearsed, whereas explaining a mechanism forces a confrontation with the limits of one's knowledge. The research suggests a modest technique for anyone hoping to defuse an acrimonious discussion. Instead of asking an opponent why they believe something, ask them how it would actually work.

Few marks of punctuation inspire as much fervor as the serial comma, the optional comma placed before the final and in a list of three or more items, as in red, white, and blue. It is often called the Oxford comma because the house style of Oxford University Press has long required it. Many newspapers, following the style guide of the Associated Press, omit it to save space. Defenders argue that the comma precludes ambiguity. Without it, a dedication to my parents, Ayn Rand and God could be read as claiming that the author's parents are Ayn Rand and God. Detractors reply that the comma can beget ambiguities of its own and that careful writers can simply rephrase ungainly sentences. The dispute might seem pedantic, but in 2017 it proved expensive. A Maine law exempted from overtime pay the canning, processing, preserving, freezing, drying, marketing, storing, packing for shipment or distribution of certain foods. Delivery drivers for a dairy company argued that no comma separated the last two items. In their reading, the law exempted packing for shipment or distribution, not distribution itself, and therefore not their work. A federal appeals court found the phrase ambiguous and sided with the drivers. The company later agreed to a settlement of five million dollars. The case became a favorite of grammar pedants, a rare instance in which a single ____ mark carried a price tag.

Once we know how a story ended, it is remarkably difficult to remember how uncertain it once seemed. In a classic study, psychologists asked students to estimate the likelihood of various possible outcomes of President Richard Nixon's 1972 visits to China and the Soviet Union, such as whether he would meet Mao Zedong. After the trips, the students were asked to recall their original estimates. Those whose predicted events had actually occurred tended to remember having assigned them higher probabilities than they really had. The phenomenon, now called hindsight bias, is sometimes summarized as the knew-it-all-along effect. It is not merely an idiosyncrasy of memory. Hindsight bias turns ordinary observers into <u>Monday-morning quarterbacks</u>, confident that a disaster was foreseeable and that those in charge must have been careless or incompetent. In experiments on legal judgments, mock jurors who learn of an accident rate it as more predictable. They also judge the defendant more negligent than jurors who evaluate the same precautions without knowing the outcome. Physicians reviewing a case are similarly swayed by knowledge of the final diagnosis. The bias also vitiates learning: if the past always appears inevitable, we draw overconfident lessons from it and underestimate the role of chance. One partial remedy is to consider the opposite, deliberately imagining how events might have unfolded differently. This restores some of the uncertainty that hindsight effaces.

For most of history, the night sky was a shared inheritance that changed only on astronomical timescales. Within a few years, it has been (A) ____ by commerce. Since the first batch of Starlink satellites was launched in 2019, the network has grown to more than six thousand spacecraft by the end of 2024, and other companies plan constellations of their own. These satellites deliver broadband internet to remote villages, ships at sea, and regions where conventional infrastructure has been destroyed, a service of palpable humanitarian value. For astronomers, however, they pose a burgeoning nuisance. Sunlit satellites passing overhead at dusk and dawn leave bright streaks across long-exposure images. The problem is especially acute for wide-field instruments such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which released its first images in 2025 and will photograph the entire southern sky every few nights. Radio astronomers report a different hazard: stray emissions from satellite electronics that can drown out faint signals from distant galaxies. Operators have responded with some (B) ____, testing darker coatings and sun visors that reduce reflected light and sharing orbital data so that observatories can schedule exposures around passing satellites. Astronomers acknowledge these efforts but warn that mitigation has limits when tens of thousands more satellites are planned. The International Astronomical Union has established a center to protect dark and quiet skies. Yet there is no binding international rule governing satellite brightness, leaving the fate of the night sky largely to the goodwill of companies and the vigilance of national regulators.

In 1990 the political scientist Joseph Nye coined the term soft power. It describes a country's ability to get what it wants through attraction rather than coercion or payment. Military strength and economic sanctions can compel, Nye argued, but a nation whose culture, values, and policies others admire can persuade without firing a shot. Governments have since sought to cultivate such influence assiduously. Britain's cultural agency has promoted the English language abroad since the 1930s, and Japan launched a Cool Japan initiative to market its animation and cuisine. South Korea, whose films, dramas, and pop music now command global audiences, has expanded its cultural centers around the world. Yet soft power resists engineering. Much of Korea's cultural success emerged from fiercely competitive private industries rather than ministerial planning, and audiences everywhere gravitate toward what feels authentic and recoil from what smells of propaganda. When culture is too visibly enlisted in the service of the state, it can prove counterproductive. China's Confucius Institutes were established on university campuses from 2004 onward to teach language and culture. They incurred suspicion that they constrained academic freedom, and many were closed in the United States and Europe. The paradox of soft power is that it tends to be most efficacious when it appears least intended.

Pick a large collection of naturally occurring numbers, such as the populations of towns or the lengths of rivers, and then look only at the first digit of each one. Intuition suggests that each digit from one to nine should lead about equally often. In fact, one appears first roughly thirty percent of the time, while nine leads fewer than five percent of the numbers. The astronomer Simon Newcomb noticed the pattern in 1881, observing that the early pages of books of logarithm tables were far more worn than the later ones. The physicist Frank Benford documented it in 1938, and the law now bears his name. Benford's law arises in data that spread across several orders of magnitude, because a quantity growing at a steady rate lingers longer among the low leading digits than among the high ones. The law does not apply to numbers assigned by people, such as telephone numbers, or to quantities confined to a narrow range, such as adult heights. Its most salient use lies in detecting fraud. People who fabricate figures tend to distribute leading digits too evenly. Auditors and tax investigators now scrutinize financial records for departures from the expected pattern. A deviation does not establish culpability, but it can tell investigators where to look more closely. Benford's law thus turns a ____ quirk of arithmetic into a tool of surprising practical value.

Why is it so much easier to give sensible advice to a friend than to follow it ourselves? Psychologists have a name for this asymmetry: Solomon's paradox, after the biblical king renowned for his wisdom yet notorious for his personal misjudgments. In a 2014 study, participants reasoned more wisely about a romantic partner's infidelity when they imagined it happening to a friend rather than to themselves. They were likelier to consider other viewpoints, acknowledge the limits of their knowledge, and seek compromise. Remarkably, the gap shrank when people were simply asked to reflect on their own dilemma in the third person. Related research on self-talk points the same way. Volunteers who prepared for a stressful speech by addressing themselves by their own name, rather than as I, reported less anxiety afterward and were later rated by observers as performing better. The researchers call this strategy self-distancing. Shifting perspective, it seems, loosens the grip of immediate emotion. It allows the reasoning we readily apply to others to be applied to ourselves. The technique is no panacea, for it cannot supply information we lack, and it may feel awkward at first. Yet the technique costs nothing at all, and it suggests that the counsel we need is often already within reach, waiting only for us to step outside our own heads.

Hosting the Olympic Games was once a prize for which cities vied fiercely. Increasingly, it looks like a burden that only a few are willing to (A) ____. The financial record is sobering. Montreal took some thirty years to pay off the debt from its 1976 Games. Researchers at the University of Oxford who examined Games held since 1960 found that every one for which reliable data exist exceeded its original budget, often by a very wide margin. Stadiums built for a few weeks of competition can become costly white elephants, and the vaunted surge in tourism frequently fails to materialize, as regular visitors avoid the crowds and inflated prices. Voters have taken notice. When bidding opened for the 2022 Winter Games, several European cities withdrew after public opposition or referendums, leaving only two candidates. The International Olympic Committee has responded by changing its approach. It now encourages hosts to use existing and temporary venues, and it invites potential hosts into informal dialogue rather than costly open contests. Paris in 2024 relied overwhelmingly on existing or temporary facilities, and Los Angeles has pledged to build no new permanent venues for 2028. Supporters argue that the Games can still serve as a catalyst for long-delayed transport and housing projects, as Barcelona's 1992 Olympics are often said to have done. Critics reply that such investments could be made more cheaply without the deadlines and security demands of a global spectacle. The emerging consensus favors a more (B) ____ model, in which the event adapts to the city rather than the city to the event.

To an English speaker, the notion that a table or a spoon should be masculine or feminine can seem whimsical. Yet in many of the world's languages, every noun belongs to a grammatical class, and that class governs the forms of the words around it. In French, a table is feminine; in German, the word for girl, Mädchen, is neuter. Nouns ending in that diminutive suffix take neuter gender regardless of meaning, a fact Mark Twain lampooned in a famous essay. Grammatical gender, linguists stress, is largely a matter of form rather than biology. Some languages divide nouns not by sex at all but into classes such as animate and inanimate, and Swahili, spoken across East Africa, partitions its nouns into more than a dozen classes. English itself once had masculine, feminine, and neuter nouns, but the distinctions eroded in the centuries after the Norman Conquest. Whether gender shapes thought is a more contentious question. One widely publicized study compared German and Spanish speakers. For German speakers bridge is feminine, and they described bridges with words such as elegant. For Spanish speakers it is masculine, and they chose words such as strong. Subsequent attempts to replicate such findings have often failed, however. Most researchers now regard any influence as subtle at best.

Few insects defend themselves as dramatically as the bombardier beetle. When threatened, it aims the tip of its abdomen at the attacker and fires a boiling, noxious spray, accompanied by an audible pop. The beetle accomplishes this feat with a two-chamber system. One reservoir holds a solution of hydroquinones and hydrogen peroxide, and when the beetle contracts its muscles, the mixture flows into a thick-walled reaction chamber. Enzymes lining this chamber decompose the peroxide almost instantly. The reaction releases enough heat to bring the liquid to about the boiling point of water, along with enough gas to blast it out. In 2015 researchers using high-speed X-ray imaging found that the spray is not continuous but pulsed, with hundreds of tiny explosions each second. Between pulses the chamber has a moment to cool, which may help the insect avoid ____ itself. The defense is remarkably efficacious. In a 2018 experiment, toads that swallowed bombardier beetles frequently vomited them up, sometimes more than an hour later. Many of the expelled beetles walked away alive. Engineers have studied the mechanism in the hope of designing more efficient fuel injectors and fire extinguishers, an example of how the solutions evolved by small creatures can inspire human technology.

Jan van Eyck's portrait of a couple standing in a lavishly furnished room rewards close looking like few other works. It was painted in 1434 and is today held by London's National Gallery. Ⓐ<u>The man</u> is usually identified as Giovanni Arnolfini, an Italian merchant living in the Flemish city of Bruges, and he raises his right hand while holding the woman's hand in his left. Every surface is rendered with astonishing precision, from the fur trim of the clothing to the oranges on the windowsill, a precision made possible by the oil glazes that Ⓑ<u>the Flemish master</u> handled with unrivaled skill. The most famous detail is a small convex mirror on the back wall. In it the couple appear from behind, and beyond them two further figures stand in the doorway, one of whom may be the painter himself. Above the mirror, an elaborate Latin inscription declares that Jan van Eyck was here, 1434. In an influential essay published in 1934, the art historian Erwin Panofsky argued that the picture records a marriage. In his view the two figures in the mirror serve as witnesses, and the inscription functions like a signature on a legal document. Many scholars now dispute this reading. Archival research has complicated the identification of Ⓒ<u>the merchant</u> and his companion. The woman's full gown was once taken as a sign of pregnancy, but she appears simply to be dressed in the fashion of the day. Who exactly is depicted, and why Ⓓ<u>Arnolfini</u> commissioned so intimate an image, may never be settled. That uncertainty has only heightened the painting's allure.

In 2020 the American Ornithological Society, which sets the official English names of birds in North America, renamed a small songbird known as McCown's longspur. The bird's namesake, a nineteenth-century army officer, had later fought for the Confederacy, and the bird became the thick-billed longspur, a name that simply describes what the bird actually looks like. Three years later the society went much further. In November 2023 it announced that it would replace the English names of all birds within its jurisdiction that honor people, roughly seventy to eighty species in all, with the work beginning in 2024. Among them are birds named for John James Audubon, the celebrated painter of birds who also enslaved people. The society argued that names honoring individuals can be ____ to potential birdwatchers. It added that descriptive names referring to plumage, song, or habitat are more useful for identifying birds in the field. The society also invited the public to take part in choosing replacements. The decision provoked acrimonious debate. Critics contended that the move effaces history. Judging historical figures by modern standards, they warned, is a slippery slope. Some noted that many honorees were obscure collectors rather than notorious villains. Supporters replied that a bird's name should tell us something about the bird rather than about the person who happened to shoot a specimen. Notably, the change applies only to English common names; the Latin scientific names, governed by a separate international code, will remain untouched.

Many listeners know the sensation: at a particular moment in a piece of music, a shiver runs down the spine and the fine hair on the arms stands on end. Researchers call these episodes chills, or frisson, and they have proved a valuable window into how the brain processes reward. In a study published in 2011, a team of neuroscientists asked volunteers to bring recordings of music that reliably gave them chills, and then scanned their brains while they listened to the music. At the moments of peak emotion, the brain released dopamine, the same chemical messenger involved in responses to food and other tangible rewards. Strikingly, dopamine release also surged in a different region during the seconds before the peak, as listeners anticipated the passage they loved. Chills tend to accompany musical surprises: an unexpected harmony, a sudden shift in volume, or the entrance of a solo voice. Composers, in other words, may elicit pleasure partly by setting up expectations and then delaying or thwarting them. Not everyone experiences chills, however. Later research found that people who do may have denser connections between the brain areas that process sound and those involved in emotion. Why should an abstract pattern of sounds, with no discernible value for survival, tap into such ancient reward circuitry? That remains an open question.

In the eighth and ninth centuries, Baghdad, the new capital of the Abbasid caliphs, became the center of one of history's most ambitious intellectual undertakings. Over roughly two hundred years, scholars translated into Arabic a vast body of Greek learning, including the works of Aristotle on logic, Galen on medicine, Euclid on geometry, and Ptolemy on astronomy. The translators often worked through intermediate translations in Syriac. The most celebrated translator, Hunayn ibn Ishaq, compared multiple manuscripts to establish reliable texts before rendering them, a practice that presaged modern scholarly editing. The patrons of the movement included caliphs, courtiers, and wealthy families. Their motives ranged from practical needs in medicine and administration to political prestige. Later accounts credit a royal library known as the House of Wisdom, although historians now debate whether it was a grand academy of learning or a more modest collection of books. The arrival of papermaking from China made books far cheaper than parchment and further fueled the enterprise. Crucially, the translators and their successors did more than ____ ancient texts. Thinkers such as the mathematician al-Khwarizmi built on Greek and Indian sources to produce original work. His name gave us the word algorithm. Much of this knowledge later reached medieval Europe through Latin translations made in Spain.

After a conversation with someone new, many of us ruminate on the exchange, wincing at an awkward pause or a joke that fell flat. A series of studies published in 2018 suggests that this self-scrutiny leads us systematically astray. Researchers paired up strangers for brief conversations and afterward asked each participant two simple questions: how much they liked their partner, and how much they thought their partner liked them. Time and again, people underestimated how much they were liked. The researchers called this discrepancy the liking gap. It appeared whether conversations lasted a few minutes or up to three-quarters of an hour. It also persisted among first-year university students who shared living quarters, narrowing only gradually over several months. Part of the explanation, the researchers proposed, is that <u>we are our own harshest critics</u>. During a conversation, we are preoccupied with monitoring our own performance. We therefore overlook the signals of warmth and interest that our partners display, signals that outside observers notice readily. Afterward, our memories dwell on our missteps rather than on the pleasant moments. The consequences may be more than emotional. If people assume they made a poor impression, they may forgo friendships or collaborations that would in fact be welcome. The findings carry an encouraging message: the stranger across the table is probably enjoying the conversation far more than we imagine, and we can afford to be gentler with ourselves.

When Pope Francis died in April 2025, the Catholic Church turned to a procedure whose essentials have changed little in centuries. Cardinals under the age of eighty, 133 of them on this occasion, gathered in the Sistine Chapel. They were sequestered from the outside world, forbidden to communicate with anyone beyond its walls until they had chosen a successor. The ordeal produced a decision, and the new pope later issued rules requiring future electors to be confined until they reached one. Today a candidate needs a two-thirds majority. After each round of voting, the ballots are burned in a stove whose chimney is visible from St. Peter's Square. Black smoke signals that no one has been elected, and white smoke signals that the church has a new leader. In May 2025 the white smoke appeared on the second day. The cardinals had chosen Robert Prevost, a Chicago-born missionary who had spent many years in Peru, and he took the name Leo XIV, becoming the first pope from the United States.
